title: In open-weight AI, America is the one playing catch-up
content:
In open-weight AI, America is the one playing catch-up
China’s best open-weight AI model has outscored America’s every day since September 2024. Even America’s best new open models typically arrive three months after a Chinese one reached the same level.
Open-weight AI models, whose weights anyone can download and run, have become China’s specialty. Labs like DeepSeek, Alibaba’s Qwen team, Zhipu and Moonshot release their strongest models openly, while most American labs keep theirs closed. Village’s LLM Atlas puts 857 models on one capability scale estimated from hundreds of public benchmarks, which lets us compare each country’s best open model day by day. By that measure, America’s open models have been behind for more than two years.
China has led every day since September 2024
- The lead has held for more than two years. Meta’s Llama 3.1 405B last matched China’s best open model in September 2024, before Alibaba’s Qwen2.5 pulled ahead.
- It is typically about five months of progress. Since 2025, China’s lead has usually been 6 to 8 points; Atlas’s frontier climbs about 1.4 points a month.
- The latest push lasted two days. Meta’s Muse Spark Open cut the lead to 2.9 points on October 15; DeepSeek’s updated V4.1 Flash widened it two days later, and Moonshot’s Kimi K3.1 Pro took it to 7 points on October 24.
The pattern repeats: the gap narrows when Meta, OpenAI or Google ships an open model, then widens when DeepSeek, Zhipu or Moonshot answers.
America’s best open models arrive months late
- Every new American record since 2025 came after China got there first. The 12 record-setting US open models arrived a median of 3.3 months after a Chinese open model reached the same score.
- Even the best showing was a month behind. Poolside’s Laguna S 2.1 came closest, at 1.1 months, in July.
More American labs are trying. Meta, Poolside and Thinking Machines have each released an open model within about three months of China’s best since July, after none did in the first half of the year. So far that has narrowed the gap without closing it.
Both still trail closed models
Neither country’s open models have caught the best closed ones. Since 2024, China’s best open models have typically trailed them by about five months, and America’s by about nine.
How we built this
This study uses Village’s LLM Atlas, which estimates one capability score per model from public benchmark results with a Bayesian item-response model, described in its methodology. For each day, we take the highest score among open-weight models each country’s labs had released by then, assigning labs to the country of their headquarters. Months behind measures how long before a model’s release a Chinese open-weight model first reached the same score. The scores are from October 31, 2026; Atlas updates as new results arrive.
Moonshot released Kimi K3.1 Pro on October 24 without weights. It is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, which Moonshot released openly, so we count it as open-weight on the assumption that its weights follow; counted as closed, China’s current lead would be 4.1 points instead of 7. Restricting to models scored on at least 10 benchmark families gives the same start date for China’s lead and similar gaps. Thirty scored models have no confirmed release date and are left out; none is an American model strong enough to have set its country’s frontier, so including them could only widen China’s lead.

report.summary: China's best open-weight models have outscored America's every day since September 2024, with new US open releases typically arriving about three months behind, according to Village's LLM Atlas.
report.background: Open-weight models are those whose parameters can be downloaded, fine-tuned and run locally, in contrast to closed models that can only be reached through an API. For the past few years, Chinese labs including DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen team, Zhipu and Moonshot have treated open releases as a core strategy: it builds developer mindshare, attracts talent and seeds entire tooling ecosystems abroad. Most American frontier labs, by contrast, keep their strongest models closed, and Meta's Llama family, long the flagship of Western open weights, has lost its lead. Village's LLM Atlas aggregates hundreds of public benchmark results into a single capability score using a Bayesian item-response model, letting analysts compare each country's best available open model on any given day rather than judging individual release announcements in isolation.
key_points: China has held the open-weight lead continuously since September 2024, when Meta's Llama 3.1 405B last matched the best Chinese open model before Alibaba's Qwen2.5 pulled ahead. The lead has persisted for more than two years across every single day tracked by the Atlas.

The gap is roughly five months of progress. Since 2025 China's advantage has usually sat at 6 to 8 Atlas points, and the frontier climbs about 1.4 points per month, meaning US labs must effectively rebuild half a year of capability to catch up.

Momentum briefly shifts but never reverses. Meta's Muse Spark Open cut the lead to 2.9 points in mid-October, only for DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash and Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro to widen it to 7 points within days. The pattern repeats: a US release narrows the gap, a Chinese answer restores it.

US records arrive late. All 12 record-setting American open models since 2025 came a median of 3.3 months after a Chinese model had already reached the same score; Poolside's Laguna S 2.1 was the closest at 1.1 months behind.

Open models still trail closed ones everywhere. China's best open models typically lag the best closed models by about five months, and America's by about nine, so the open-weight race is not the same as the frontier race.
report.impact: The findings reframe a narrative that has often cast China as the imitator. If Chinese labs consistently ship open weights months ahead of their US counterparts, developers worldwide building on downloadable models will increasingly default to Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi and Zhipu checkpoints, which shapes fine-tuning ecosystems, tooling and even downstream research agendas. American labs face a strategic tension: open weights spread influence but can be copied, while closed APIs protect revenue but cede the open ecosystem. For regular users, the practical effect is cheaper, more capable local models, more self-hosting options and less dependence on a single vendor's API. For policymakers, the data suggests export controls and compute restrictions have not prevented Chinese labs from leading in the open-weight category, which may intensify scrutiny of open release practices on both sides.
report.tools: To follow this yourself, start with Village's LLM Atlas, which publishes daily cross-country capability comparisons. Complement it with Hugging Face (where Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi checkpoints land first), the LMArena leaderboard for human-preference rankings, Artificial Analysis for speed and price comparisons, and OpenRouter for trying many models through one interface. For hands-on testing, Ollama and vLLM let you run open-weight models locally or serve them at scale, and the Open LLM Leaderboard remains a useful sanity check on benchmark claims.
